newsitem.title: USA: U.S. yield curve seen flattening sharply - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. yield curve seen flattening sharply - Merrill.

text.p: The U.S. yield curve is expected to flatten sharply over the next six months with the spread between the two-year note and the 30-year bond adopting a flat posture or even becoming slightly inverted, said Thomas Sowanick, chief fixed-income strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"I think ... we could have a pretty sharp flattening of the yield curve," Sowanick said in an telephone interview.

"Right now (the spread between) twos and 30s is at 74 (basis points). I think that we have a very strong chance that the curve moves in all the way to a flat posture, to even slightly inverted ... over the course of the next six months or so," Sowanick said.

Sowanick said Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins congressional testimony on Wednesday suggested some inflation pressures might be building and that the central bank might raise rates pre-emptively.

"He turned the page a bit, one, suggesting that there may be some inflation pressures building and two, that they (Fed officials) would be pre-emptive. I think he's warning us of a prospect for a tightening rather than an ease," Sowanick said.

Greenspan delivered the first leg of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday. The chairman said, among other things, that he sees upside inflation risks and that he could not rule out a pre-emptive tightening.
Sowanick also said he believes the U.S. money market has not yet priced in much Fed tightening.
"The market still has not priced in much of a Fed move," Sowanick said, adding that he expects "the biggest move in rates, or the largest chunk of it ... in the second quarter."
